subject: chemistry
title: Limiting reactants
key_idea: The reactant that is completely used up is the limiting reactant. It limits the amount of product, and the reaction stops when it runs out. The mass of product depends on the limiting reactant, not the reactant in excess.

blocks.text: (Higher tier) Reactants are not always mixed in the exact amounts the equation needs. One reactant usually runs out first.

items.meaning: The reactant that is completely used up. It limits the amount of product.
A reactant that is left over when the reaction stops.

items: Chemists often use an excess of one reactant to make sure all of the other reactant is used up.
When the limiting reactant is used up, the reaction stops.
The mass of product is controlled by the reactant that is **not** in excess.
Adding more of the excess reactant does not make more product.

blocks.text: Why the reaction slows and stops

items: As the reaction goes on, there are fewer particles of the limiting reactant in the mixture.
Collisions between the reacting particles become less frequent, so the rate decreases.
The reaction stops when the limiting reactant is used up.
Solid left over at the end shows that the solid was in excess. For example, marble chips left in acid mean the acid was the limiting reactant.
The limiting reactant is used up first and limits the amount of product.
The reaction stops when the limiting reactant runs out.
A reactant left over at the end is the one in excess.

blocks.text: (Higher tier) Compare the amounts in moles, not the masses. The balanced equation tells you how many moles of one reactant react with each mole of another.

blocks.label: Amount in moles
where: moles is the amount of substance in mol
Mr is the relative formula mass

items.text: Work out the moles of each reactant from its mass.
Use the equation to find the moles of the second reactant needed to react with all of the first.
If there are fewer moles than are needed, that reactant is the limiting reactant.
The other reactant is in excess.

blocks.text: 4.8 g of magnesium burns in 8.0 g of oxygen. 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16.

items.text: 2 mol Mg reacts with 1 mol O₂, so 0.20 mol Mg needs 0.10 mol O₂.
0.25 mol O₂ is more than the 0.10 mol needed. Oxygen is in excess and magnesium is the limiting reactant.

diagram.alt: Practise finding the moles of hydrogen made when one of two reactants is limiting.
diagram.question: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. **{a}** mol of magnesium reacts with **{b}** mol of hydrochloric acid. Calculate the maximum amount of hydrogen made, in mol.
working: 1 mol of Mg makes 1 mol of H₂. 2 mol of HCl also makes 1 mol of H₂.
Mg could make {a} mol of H₂. HCl could make {b} ÷ 2 mol of H₂.
The smaller amount is the limit: **{answer}** mol of H₂.

items: Convert masses to moles before comparing reactants.
Use the ratio in the equation to see which reactant is short.
The reactant that would run out first is the limiting reactant.

sections.heading: Mass of product from the limiting reactant

blocks.text: (Higher tier) The maximum mass of product is found from the limiting reactant, never from the excess.

blocks.label: Mass of product
where: moles is the moles of product, found from the limiting reactant and the equation ratio
Mr is the relative formula mass of the product

items.text: Use the equation ratio from the limiting reactant to the product.
Multiply the moles of product by its Mr.

blocks.text: In the example above, 0.20 mol Mg makes 0.20 mol MgO (a 2 : 2 ratio). Mr of MgO = 40, so the mass is 0.20 × 40 = 8.0 g.

diagram.alt: Practise finding the maximum mass of magnesium oxide from masses of magnesium and oxygen.
diagram.question: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. **{m}** g of magnesium reacts with **{o}** g of oxygen. Calculate the maximum mass of magnesium oxide made. Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16.
working: Moles of Mg = {m} ÷ 24. Moles of O₂ = {o} ÷ 32.
2 mol Mg make 2 mol MgO. 1 mol O₂ makes 2 mol MgO.
The smaller amount of MgO limits the reaction. Mass = moles of MgO × 40 = **{answer}** g.

items: Work out the product from the limiting reactant only.
Mass = moles of product × Mr of product.

sections.heading: Using masses to find an equation

blocks.text: (Higher tier) The masses of reactants and products give the moles of each. The ratio of the moles is the ratio of the numbers in the balanced equation.

items.text: Divide by the smallest number of moles. If the ratio is not whole numbers, multiply to make it whole.
Use the ratio as the numbers in front of the formulae.

blocks.text: Example: 2.7 g of aluminium (Ar = 27) reacts with excess copper chloride to make 9.525 g of copper (Ar = 63.5).

items: Moles of Al = 2.7 ÷ 27 = 0.10 mol. Moles of Cu = 9.525 ÷ 63.5 = 0.15 mol.
The ratio Al : Cu is 0.10 : 0.15, which is 1 : 1.5. Multiply by 2 to get 2 : 3.
So the equation is 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 3Cu + 2AlCl₃.
Moles of each substance come from mass ÷ Mr.
The mole ratio gives the numbers in the balanced equation.

checks.q: What is meant by the term limiting reactant?
checks.a: The reactant that is used up first (completely used up in the reaction). It limits the amount of product, so the reaction stops when it runs out.

checks.q: Marble chips are left in the flask when a reaction with hydrochloric acid stops. Explain why the reaction stops.
checks.a: All of the acid has been used up. The acid is the limiting reactant and the marble chips are in excess.

checks.q: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. 0.30 mol of magnesium reacts with 0.50 mol of hydrochloric acid. Which is the limiting reactant, and how many moles of hydrogen are made?
checks.a: 0.30 mol Mg needs 0.60 mol HCl, but only 0.50 mol is present, so hydrochloric acid is the limiting reactant. 0.50 ÷ 2 = 0.25 mol of H₂ is made.

exam_phrases: (identifying limiting reactant) 4 moles Al gives 6 moles Cu; 8.996 moles CuCl2 gives 8.996 moles Cu
therefore aluminium is the limiting reactant
37.0 mol is less than the (2 × 18.75 =) 37.5 mol (aluminium needed)
iron oxide is in excess because 18.75 mol is more than the (37.0/2 =) 18.5 mol (iron oxide needed)
fewer particles (of acid / magnesium) as reaction progresses
reaction stops due to limiting factor / reagent

mistakes.wrong: The reaction stops because the reactants are used up.
mistakes.right: Name the reactant. Say the (hydrochloric) acid is used up, or that it is the limiting reactant. 'Reactants used up' alone is ignored.

mistakes.wrong: The rate decreases because there are fewer collisions.
mistakes.right: 'Fewer collisions' alone is ignored. Say there are fewer particles, so the collisions are less frequent.

mistakes.wrong: Iron oxide is limiting because 18.75 mol of Fe₂O₃ is fewer moles than 37.0 mol of Al.
mistakes.right: Use the 2 : 1 ratio in the equation. 18.75 mol of Fe₂O₃ needs 2 × 18.75 = 37.5 mol of Al, but only 37.0 mol is present, so aluminium is limiting.

worked_example.question:
A mixture contains 1.00 kg of aluminium and 3.00 kg of iron oxide.

The equation for the reaction is:

2 Al + Fe₂O₃ → 2 Fe + Al₂O₃

Relative atomic masses (Ar): O = 16, Al = 27, Fe = 56

Show that aluminium is the limiting reactant.
answer_points: Aluminium is limiting because 37.0 mol is less than the 37.5 mol (2 × 18.75) needed. Or iron oxide is in excess because 18.75 mol is more than the 18.5 mol (37.0 ÷ 2) needed.
worked_example.tip: One mark each. Change kg to g, find the moles of both, then use the 2 : 1 ratio to compare.

exam_phrases: the equation shows two HCl reacting with one Mg
1 mol HCl reacts with 0.5 mol of Mg
0.5 mol HCl reacts with 0.25 mol Mg

mistakes.wrong: 0.5 mol of HCl and 0.5 mol of Mg are the same amount, so both are used up.
mistakes.right: The equation has 2 HCl for every 1 Mg. 0.5 mol of HCl reacts with only 0.25 mol of Mg, so magnesium is in excess.

mistakes.wrong: Magnesium is in excess because there is more magnesium.
mistakes.right: Say why, using the ratio. The equation shows two HCl reacting with one Mg, so 1 mol of HCl needs only 0.5 mol of Mg.

worked_example.question:
The balanced equation for a reaction is
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂

In a further experiment, 0.5 mol of hydrochloric acid, HCl, were mixed with 0.5 mol of magnesium, Mg.
Use the equation to show that, in this experiment, the magnesium is in excess.
answer_points: The equation shows two HCl reacting with one Mg (ratio 2 : 1).
So 0.5 mol of HCl reacts with only 0.25 mol of Mg, and magnesium is in excess.
worked_example.tip: The mark is for the 2 : 1 ratio. Say it, then use it with the amounts given.

exam_phrases: limiting reactant is the reactant that is used up first
limiting reactant has fewer moles (than other reactants)
reaction stops once limiting reactant is consumed or used up
marble chips are left over at the end of the reaction / marble chips are in excess
all the (dilute hydrochloric) acid was used up

mistakes.wrong: The reaction stops because the marble is used up.
mistakes.right: This is ignored. Say all of the dilute hydrochloric acid was used up, or that the acid was the limiting reactant.

mistakes.wrong: The student can tell the acid is limiting because it was used up first.
mistakes.right: This is ignored. Say marble chips are left over at the end, so the marble chips are in excess.
Convert cm³ to dm³ first by dividing by 1000. Using cm³ instead of dm³ gives only 1 mark for the two moles calculations.

worked_example.question:
A student reacts sodium hydroxide solution with dilute hydrochloric acid.

NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O

35.0 cm³ of 0.075 mol / dm³ hydrochloric acid, HCl, are added to 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol / dm³ sodium hydroxide solution, NaOH.

Use the information to determine which reactant is in excess.
answer_points: The acid is in excess (the ratio is 1 : 1, and there are more moles of acid).
worked_example.tip: Convert each volume to dm³ and work out both amounts in moles before you compare them.
